newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's PRI elects a canny Zedillo ally as leader.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's PRI elects a canny Zedillo ally as leader.

text.p: Humberto Roque Villanueva, the new leader of Mexico's ruling party, is known as a astute, string-pulling politician with the firm backing of President Ernesto Zedillo.

Roque was elected on Sunday as president of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has governed the country for 67 years. Santiago Onate Labourde stepped down from the post on Friday after 16 months.
"How's the party doing, Humberto?," Zedillo is said to have asked the graying 53-year-old at a dinner on Friday night when it emerged that Roque was to be the new party leader.
"Fine, sir," Roque answered, according to newspapers, which reported the conversation third-hand.

"But it could be doing better ... put yourself in charge of that," Zedillo is said to have replied, putting his faith in a friend who will lead the PRI in the run-up to crucial mid-term elections next summer.

Zedillo and Roque are solid allies. "For me, the most important, most prestigious asset that the PRI counts on is called Ernesto Zedillo," Roque has said, leaving no doubt about his support for the president.

Like Zedillo, Roque has a strong background in economics. Born in the northern industrial city of Torreon, Roque graduated from the National Autonomous University in Mexico City in 1970 with a degree in economics.

He went on to teach economic development theory at the university, Mexico's biggest college and a political hotbed. At the same time, he began engineering a political career by building a network of contacts.
Most of his political activism has been inside the National Campesino Confederation (CNC), a highly politicized peasant organisation linked to the ruling party.

He also held posts in the Agriculture and Fishing ministries. Until this week, he was leader of the PRI majority in the lower house of congress, where he gained a reputation as a string-pulling insider who had opened up lines of communication and negotiation with opposition parties.
"He is a politician who has demonstrated his great conciliation capacity," said PRI legislator Jose Lanz.
But Mexicans recognise him as the politician who recently made an uncouth gesture uncouthly in front of TV cameras when he failed to control his emotions on winning a tense vote to raise taxes.
For the moment that image is forgotten. Sunday's newspapers splashed his face across front pages, gesturing the "V" for victory and all smiles.
